How to Dispose of Old Fence

Whether your garden’s looking a little cramped, your neighbor’s new fence has left yours outdated, or you’ve finally decided it’s time for a makeover, figuring out what to do with that old fence can feel like a puzzle. The good news? You’ve got plenty of options—from DIY recycling to letting the pros at 1-800‑GOT‑JUNK? handle the heavy lifting. Let’s walk through each step so you can choose the most cost‑effective, environmentally‑friendly path.

1. Assess the Condition of Your Fence

Is it reusable or beyond repair?

Take a close look at the wood, metal, or vinyl panels. If the boards are still solid, free of rot, and the metal isn’t rusted through, you might be able to repurpose them. If the fence is splintered, warped, or coated with lead‑based paint, it’s safer to dispose of it as junk.

What materials are you dealing with?

  • Wood: Often recyclable or reusable.
  • Metal (steel/aluminum): Highly recyclable.
  • Vinyl: Typically ends up in a landfill unless a specialty recycler is available.

2. Check Local Regulations

Every municipality has its own rules about fence disposal. Some cities require a permit for removal, while others have designated drop‑off sites for bulky waste. A quick call to your local public works department can save you from unexpected fines.

Typical restrictions to watch for

  • Size limits for curbside pickup (often 6‑8 feet in length).
  • Prohibited materials (e.g., treated wood with hazardous chemicals).
  • Specific days for bulk trash collection.

3. DIY Disposal Options

Donate or Give Away

If your fence is still in decent shape, consider posting it on community boards, Craigslist, or a local “Freecycle” group. Hobbyists love reclaimed wood for projects, and a metal fence can be a treasure for DIY‑savvy neighbors.

Recycle It

Many recycling centers accept wood and metal. Call ahead to confirm acceptance and any preparation steps (e.g., removing nails). Some centers even pay a small fee for metal scrap, turning your old fence into a modest cash boost.

Bulk Trash Pickup

Check whether your town offers a bulk trash service. You’ll usually need to schedule a pickup, and there may be a per‑item fee. This method is straightforward but can be pricey if you have a long fence.

Rent a Dumpster

For large projects, a short‑term dumpster rental (often a 10‑yard size) can be economical. Just be mindful of weight limits—metal can get heavy fast.

4. When to Call a Professional Junk Removal Service

Sometimes the easiest route is to let the experts handle it. Here’s when dialing up 1-800‑GOT‑JUNK? makes sense:

  • Time constraints: You need the fence gone today.
  • Safety concerns: The fence is high, unstable, or located near power lines.
  • Volume: The fence is longer than a typical curbside pickup can manage.
  • Environmental peace of mind: 1-800‑GOT‑JUNK? sorts and recycles what it can, diverting waste from landfills.

Professional removal eliminates the guesswork, and a simple phone call can get a team on your property within 24‑48 hours. Plus, you’ll avoid any hidden fees for disposal—everything is included in one transparent price.

5. Step‑by‑Step Guide to DIY Fence Removal

Gather the right tools

  • Safety glasses and gloves
  • Reciprocating saw or handsaw (for wood)
  • Bolt cutters (for metal)
  • Hammer or pry bar
  • Wheelbarrow or dolly for moving sections

Safety first

Turn off any nearby utilities, especially if the fence runs close to electrical lines. Wear sturdy boots and keep a clear work area to avoid trips.

Disassembly process

  1. Remove posts: Dig around the base with a post‑hole digger or shovel. Loosen the soil and pry the post out.
  2. Detach panels: Unscrew or cut any fasteners. For wood, a reciprocating saw can speed up the process.
  3. Separate materials: Stack wood separate from metal to simplify recycling later.

Transport and disposal

Load the sections onto a truck or trailer. If you’re heading to a recycling center, keep the metal together and the wood in a separate pile. If you’re using curbside pickup, break larger pieces into manageable sizes (under 6 feet) to meet local size limits.
